questions.question_text: An important risk factor for depression and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation:
Symptoms of hypothyroidism include weakness, fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and somnolence. Psychiatric
symptoms  include depression (often misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder and hypothyroidism may be missed), also cognitive
dysfunction is noted. Psychosis may be seen in severe cases (myxedema madness). Subclinical hypothyroidism is a risk factor for depression
and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: The male: female ratio of hypothyroidism is
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism is more common in women than in men (in t he UK, female:male ratio of 6:1).

questions.question_text: Hoover's test is a type of physical examination done to identify the possible diagnosis of
questions.explanation:
Hoover's test is useful to identify patients with conversion disorder, who has paralysis with One or more limbs or one side of the face or
body may be a�ected. Here the patient is unable to raise the a�ected limb from the couch but is able to raise the una�ected limb against
resistance with demonstrable pressing down of the heel on the a�ected side. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 746

questions.question_text: The clinical feature that is most suggestive of herpes simplex encephalitis is
questions.explanation:
Herpes simplex encephalitis: Fairly abrupt onset of confusion, memory impairment, and often seizures. 70% show psychiatric disturbances
including acute confusion, depression and psychosis. Fever is common but not invariable.

questions.question_text:
A woman who has had Herpes encephalitis develops severe carbohydrate craving, weight gain and inappropriate sexuality. Which of the
following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Herpes simplex encephalitis: HSE is the most common cause of Kluver Bucy syndrome in humans; this is characterized by emotional
blunting, hyperphagia, visual agnosia and inappropriate sexual behaviour. This is due to bilateral temporal lobe damage and most often only
a partial syndrome is evident. Carbamazepine may be used to control some symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Meige's syndrome is incorrect?

options.text: The movement is present both at rest and when active
Oral facial dystonia characterized by repetitive blinking and chin thrusting
The patients are more likely to be middle-aged men than women

correct_answer.text: The patients are more likely to be middle-aged men than women

questions.explanation:
Henri Meige described in 1904 a new type of oral facial dystonia characterized by repetitive blinking and chin thrusting. Some patients have
lip pursing or tongue movements and, for a few, the movements spread into the shoulders. Primary Meige's is idiopathic; antipsychotics,
levodopa and Lewy body dementia can cause secondary Meige's. At times there is a joint interactive movement between the oral
movements and the eye movements. The patients are more likely to be women than men and usually at middle age. There is some variation
with stress, but the movement is present both at rest and when active; it disappears with sleep. Patients may chew gum, whistle or touch
their face in an e�ort to lessen the movements (Retrieved from

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a weak inhibitor of cytochrome P450 enzyme system?
questions.explanation:
Fluoxetine and Paroxetine are potent inhibitors of hepatic CYP enzyme systems (CYP2D6, CYP3A4). Sertraline is a less potent inhibitor but
this e�ect is dose related; at higher doses that are commonly used in practice, sertraline may induce clinically important inhibition of the
CYP system. Citalopram is a weak inhibitor. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 336

questions.question_text:
Some patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder with the primary aim
of obtaining medical attention and treatment. Which of the following diagnosis is most appropriate in these circumstances?
questions.explanation:
Factitious disorder (Munchausen's Syndrome): In factitious disorder patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history and
fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. The diagnostic features are
the intentional and conscious production of signs, falsi�cation, or exaggeration of the history and the lack of gain beyond medical attention
and treatment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor associated with depression in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation:
Depression in Parkinson's disease: Risk factors include Female sex, younger onset, prominent right-sided signs, bradykinesia and gait
disturbance, rapid disease progression, poorer cognitive status and activities of daily living. Apathy without depression is also common and
is associated with executive dysfunction. It may be masked by Parkinsonian a�ect - subjective exploration may be necessary.

questions.question_text: All are true about delirium in palliative care except

options.text: Occurs in over 50% of patients at some stage in their illness

questions.explanation:
Delirium is common in palliative care settings. The prevalence is around 44% in cancer in-patients, rising to 62% shortly before death. It may
be either hypoactive sedated subtype or hyperactive agitated type. The aetiology is usually multi-factorial, and a speci�c aetiology is
discovered in less than 50% of terminally ill patients with delirium. Though small dose of haloperidol or lorazepam is frequently used, they
are not always successful in controlling the symptoms, especially in sedated subtype.

questions.question_text: Poor prognostic factors with respect to psychiatric morbidity following head injury include all except

options.text: Long period of post traumatic amnesia
Long duration of loss of consciousness
Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe

correct_answer.text: Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe

questions.explanation:
After a head injury, patients who struggle to return to previous activities generally report a longer duration of post-traumatic amnesia and
loss of consciousness than those who resume work without much di�culties. Focal non-dominant lobe damage does not indicate poor
prognosis.

questions.question_text:
Mr.Y su�ers from psychiatric symptoms such as apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. He reports repeated vomiting. On
examination you discover unexplained dark skin pigmentation. This should suggest
questions.explanation:
Addison's disease: (Cortisol depletion) Psychiatric symptoms - apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. May be misdiagnosed as
major depressive disorder. Anorexia is common in both, but the presence of nausea, vomiting and skin changes (dark pigmentation in some)
should suggest Addison's disease.

questions.question_text:
A proportion of patients who are at a high risk of HIV are seronegative but remain anxious about contracting HIV. Which of the following
descriptions/diagnosis suits them best?
questions.explanation:
The term "worried well" refers to someone who harbours a fear that he or she has the disease or may contract the infection imminently.  
 Some of the charactersitics of the worried well include: 
Several negative HIV tests
Poor sexual adjustment and social isolation
Multiple somatic features wrongly interpreted as a part of an undiagnosed HIV illness  
Psychiatric history - especially anxiety or depression 
Ref: Chippindale & French., BMJ. 2001 Jun 23; 322(7301): 1533-1535.

questions.question_text:
Depression is thought to be the most common mental illness in those with HIV infection. Which of the following is least likely to explain the
high rates of depression noted in HIV-infected individuals?

options.text: Shared risk factors in the two groups
Spuriously high diagnosis due to shared symptomatology

questions.explanation:
The risk factors for depression are similar to the risk factors for those without HIV. These include; A. advanced HIV infection: B. loss of social
support; C. personal and family history of depression; D. drug use; and E. lack of con�dants. Poor adherence to medical treatment for HIV
can occur as a result of depression, complicating management. Antiretroviral therapy is not a common cause of depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications has the best evidence for use in HIV dementia complex?
questions.explanation: Patients with HIV dementia may stabilize or improve slightly on antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine has the best evidence in this regard).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a primary organic disorder due to HIV infection?
questions.explanation:
Neuropsychiatric disorders in HIV can be either primary organic (directly due to viral CNS damage) e.g. HIV dementia or secondary organic
(due to opportunistic infections or drugs) e.g. cerebral toxoplasmosis or reactive e.g. HIV associated acute stress reaction. Prevalance of any
mental disorder in the lifetime of HIV positive patients is 38 to 73%.

questions.question_text: The most frequent cause of psychiatric hospitalisation in those with HIV seropositivity is
questions.explanation:
HIV seems to increase the risk of manic episodes, and mania is the most frequent reason for psychiatric hospitalization among people with
HIV, followed by depression and psychosis.

questions.question_text:
A 34 year old homosexual man presents with forgetfulness, loss of concentration, mental slowing. He admits to unsafe sexual practices. He
appears clumsy and apathetic. Which of the following statements is false with regard to his diagnosis?

options.text: Laboratory evidence of HIV infection is necessary to make the diagnosis
Aphasia, agnosia and apraxia are unusual
Decline in motor function may be present
The minimum duration of symptoms must be 1 year to make the diagnosis
Decline in memory may not be severe enough to impair all ADLs

correct_answer.text: The minimum duration of symptoms must be 1 year to make the diagnosis

questions.explanation: Dementia is noted concurrently with initial AIDS-de�ning illness in 3% of cases. 1-month duration is su�cient

questions.question_text: The most common neuropsychiatric symptom associated with Parkinson's disease is
questions.explanation:
While depression may be partly reactive to receiving the diagnosis or experiencing a worsening of PD symptoms, the depressive illness may
be due to the actual disease process itself. Depression in PD is very frequent (50%) and is more common in women and is often atypical in
nature.

questions.question_text: In patients with transient global amnesia, the amnesic episode usually resolves within
questions.explanation:
Transient global amnesia is characterized by the abrupt onset anterograde amnesia characterized by signi�cant new learning de�cit"
(Excerpt from Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry). Patients show mild confusion and a lack of insight into the problem but an intact sensorium.
Episodes last from 6 to 24 hours. Though the aetiology is unclear, most cases involve hypoperfusion in the temporal and parietotemporal
regions, particularly in the left hemisphere. Most patients show complete improvement though recurrence is high.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments for MS is most likely to lead to depression?
questions.explanation:
Though controversial, only a weak association has been reported with beta interferon. Note that among the various interferons, it is
Interferon alpha which is clearly associated with depression (used in viral hepatitis).

questions.question_text: In post-stroke depression, the antidepressant treatment should be continued for at least
questions.explanation:
There is limited evidence regarding the e�cacy of antidepressants in treating post-stroke depression.Although there is the suggestion that
Tricyclic antidepressants are more e�ective, SSRIs are a reasonable �rst choice. Consider a trial of antidepressant medication in those with a
persistently depressed mood of at least 1-month duration. If there is a good response, antidepressants should be continued for at least 6
months.

questions.question_text: What is the mean duration of a major depressive episode that follows a stroke?
questions.explanation: The mean duration of post-stroke, major depression is 34 weeks

questions.question_text:
A 42-year-old woman presents with a history of 2 episodes of unilateral blindness that lasted for few weeks. Now she has paraesthesia of
left leg and appears quite depressed. Her MRI brain shows multiple demyelinating plaques. With respect to her depression which of the
following is NOT correct?

options.text: Has a lifetime prevalence of up to 50% in those with the same neurological condition
Can be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy
Can be caused by the drugs used to treat the neurological condition

questions.explanation:
The description is suggestive of multiple sclerosis. A 20% risk of triggering a relapse of multiple sclerosis has been reported if ECT is given.
The presence of active brain lesions on MRI before treatment is a potential risk factor for MS relapse following ECT. But MS is not an
absolute contraindication for ECT administration.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following cognitive faculties remains intact in amnestic disorders?
questions.explanation:
The Amnestic disorders are syndromes characterised by the development of a memory disorder characterized by impairment in the ability
to learn new information (anterograde amnesia) and the inability to recall previously remembered knowledge (retrograde amnesia). A
general medical condition or use substance usually causes it, and where delirium and dementia have been excluded as causative of the
amnesia. In amnesic disorders, short-term and recent memory is usually impaired. Memory for events from the remote past, such as
childhood experiences, is generally retained, but the memory for events from the less remote past (over the past decade) is impaired.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning cognitive impairment seen in multiple sclerosis?

options.text: Is no more common than in the general population
Can be explained by the increased prevalence of depression in multiple sclerosis
Has the same feature as a subcortical dementia
Is best screened for using the Mini-Mental State Examination

correct_answer.text: Has the same feature as a subcortical dementia

questions.explanation:
Subcortical dementia is "a clinical syndrome characterized by slowness of mental processing, forgetfulness, impaired cognition, apathy, and
depression. First recognized in progressive supranuclear palsy and Huntington's disease, the concept has been extended to account for the
intellectual impairment of Parkinson's disease, Wilson's disease, spinocerebellar degenerations, idiopathic basal ganglia calci�cation, the
lacunar state, and the dementia syndrome of MS"(Excerpt from Cummings, J. L., & Benson, D. F. (1984). Subcortical dementia: Review of an
emerging concept. Archives of Neurology, 41(8), 874-879.).

questions.question_text: With respect to management of Parkinson's disease which of the following is correct?

options.text: Dementia can be treated with any Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors as RCT evidence is abundant
Hypomania is a side e�ect of levodopa
Clozapine must be avoided in Parkinsons psychosis
Psychosis is associated with decreases in antiparkinsonian medications
Quetiapine is best avoided among all antipsychotics

correct_answer.text: Hypomania is a side e�ect of levodopa

questions.explanation:
Psychosis in Parkinson's disease is mostly drug related with both dopaminergic/anticholinergic medications being implicated. Hallucinations
are common ( 20% ) especially in visual modality.

questions.question_text: The frequency of depressive symptoms in epilepsy is
questions.explanation: Psychiatric symptoms in epilepsy: Depression- 30-50%, Panic disorder- 20%, Psychosis- 3-7%

questions.question_text:
A 42-year-old man su�ering from poorly controlled epilepsy is referred by the neurologist as non-epileptic seizures are suspected. Which of
the following statement is correct?

options.text: Non epileptic seizures are more common in males
Prolactin levels are elevated after non-epileptic attack
Video recording of ictal and periictal behaviour can help in diagnosis
Known epileptic patients do not have dissociative seizures
Presence of depression suggests non-epileptic attacks in most epileptics.

correct_answer.text: Video recording of ictal and periictal behaviour can help in diagnosis

questions.explanation:
Pseudoseizures (Non epileptic seizures) are often associated with past psychiatric history. Pseudoseizures more likely to happen in the
daytime and when others are present. Increased post-ictal serum prolactin concentrations (greater than 1000 IU/l) despite normal baseline
levels are found after epileptic seizures but measurements must be taken within 15 min of the event. Video recording along with EEG is the
best diagnostic measure.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following drugs is particularly epileptogenic and should be used with caution in epileptic psychosis?
questions.explanation:
Prevalence of psychosis in epilepsy is between 3 and 7%. It is more common in those with partial epilepsies. Haloperidol and Sulpiride may
be less epileptogenic than other antipsychotics and, therefore, the treatment of choice for epileptic psychosis. Clozapine can worsen
epileptic psychosis by lowering seizure threshold.

questions.question_text: Post-traumatic epilepsy is seen in what proportion of patients with open head injury?
questions.explanation:
Post-traumatic epilepsy is seen in 5% closed and 30% open head injuries (usually during �rst year) and worsens prognosis. Less
psychopathology in children after head injury due to increased brain plasticity.

questions.question_text: Post-concussional syndrome is characterized by all except;
questions.explanation:
Post-concussional syndrome is characterized by headache, dizziness, fatigue, poor memory, poor concentration, irritability, depression,
sleep disturbance, frustration, restlessness, sensitivity to noise, blurred vision, double vision, photophobia, nausea and tinnitus (King, 1997).
At least 50% experience some post-concussion symptoms that recover completely within 3 months of injury, except in nearly a third.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false about mania seen in multiple sclerosis?

options.text: Is more common than in the general population
Predominant frontal distribution of plaques in MRI
Can be induced by prescribed treatments for multiple sclerosis
Can occur as part of the primary physical disorder.

correct_answer.text: Predominant frontal distribution of plaques in MRI

questions.explanation:
People with multiple sclerosis who become hypomanic on steroid therapy are more likely to have a family or premorbid history of a�ective
disorder and/or alcoholism. There is MRI evidence suggesting that patients showing mania with psychotic symptoms have plaques that are
distributed predominantly in the bilateral temporal horn areas

questions.question_text:
A 45-year-old gentleman was admitted to the medical unit with history of stroke. A psychiatric opinion was requested due to his
deteriorating mental state. His MRI brain scan showed lesions proximal to the left frontal lobe. Which one of the following psychiatric
conditions is most likely to occur in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
According to a meta-analytic study by Narushima et, al. 2003, the proximity of the lesions to the left frontal lobe predicts depressive illness.
This is also supported by another study from Finland (Vataja et al. 2004).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about mania in multiple sclerosis is incorrect?

options.text: There is MRI evidence suggesting that patients showing mania with psychotic symptoms have plaques that are distributed
predominantly in the bilateral temporal horn areas
Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 2/3rd of patients given steroids.
Higher than expected prevalence of mania
People with multiple sclerosis who become hypomanic on steroid therapy are more likely to have a family history of a�ective disorder.

correct_answer.text: Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 2/3rd of patients given steroids.

questions.explanation:
Mania in multiple sclerosis: Higher than expected prevalence of mania. It can also be drug induced: steroids (more likely), baclofen,
dantrolene, tizanidine (central muscle relaxant). Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 1/3rd of patients given steroids. People
with multiple sclerosis who become hypomanic on steroid therapy are more likely to have a family or premorbid history of a�ective disorder
and/or alcoholism. There is MRI evidence suggesting that patients showing mania with psychotic symptoms have plaques that are
distributed predominantly in the bilateral temporal horn areas

questions.question_text:
A psychiatric trainee is keen to obtain prolactin concentrations from a patient to determine possibility of a true seizure activity. What is the
time limit after a seizure within which the measurements must be taken?
questions.explanation:
Increased post-ictal serum prolactin concentrations (greater than 1000 IU/l) despite normal baseline levels are found after epileptic seizures
but measurements must be taken within 15 min of the event.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime prevalence of depressive symptoms in patients with multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
In patients with multiple sclerosis, lifetime prevalence of depressive symptoms is reported in 40-50%. It is about three times higher than the
rate in the general population. Desipramine and SSRIs have an evidence base for their use in the treatment. ECT may be used. However,
there is a 20% risk of triggering a relapse of multiple sclerosis if ECT is given

questions.question_text:
A 65-year-old gentleman with Parkinson's disease presented with psychotic symptoms characterized by paranoia and visual hallucinations.
His wife does not want his antiparkinsonian medication to be stopped as it has worsened the motor features of Parkinsons disease in the
past. Which antipsychotic can improve his symptoms without worsening Parkinsonism?
questions.explanation:
In parkinsonian psychosis, consideration should be given to decreasing or stopping antiparkinsonian drugs. Due to the propensity to cause
EPSEs antipsychotic medications should be used with caution. There is good evidence that low dose clozapine (less than 100 mg/day) can
improve psychosis without worsening parkinsonism (Parkinson study group 1999).

questions.question_text: The gene for Huntington's disease (HD) is located on which chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Huntington's disease can manifest at any time between infancy and senescence. The mutant protein in Huntington's disease—huntingtin—
results from an expanded CAG repeat leading to a polyglutamine strand of variable length at the N-terminus. This tail confers a toxic gain of
function. The gene for Huntington's disease (HD) is located on the short arm of chromosome four and is associated with an expanded
trinucleotide repeat.

questions.question_text: Head injury may predispose to the development of
questions.explanation:
Head injuries, particularly in men, may predispose to the development of Alzheimers disease. (Fleminger et al 2003). It is possibly due to
deposition of beta amyloid in the brain at the time of the injury, although evidence that it is linked to APOE status is inconsistent. Head injury
has long been considered as a possible risk factor for schizophrenia although a comprehensive critical review of psychosis following head
injury concludes that the injury is unlikely to be a causal factor in the disorder (David and Prince 2005; Advances in neuropsychiatry: clinical
implications | BJPsych. Retrieved from  Nevertheless, 'psychosis' is known to occur after head
injuries.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a history of epileptic psychosis and remains psychotic. The most appropriate drug of choice is;
questions.explanation: Drug-induced low mood is an important di�erential diagnosis

questions.question_text: The psychiatric syndrome most commonly associated with stroke is
questions.explanation:
Depressive illness after stroke is extremely common, occurring in up to 50-60% of cases. Its onset is usually between 3 and 24 months
following the stroke.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Z has a history of epilepsy and has now been diagnosed with depression. Which class of drugs should be used as �rst a line treatment
in her case?
questions.explanation:
Depression in epilepsy is mainly associated with the location of lesion - esp. common in TLE. High risk of suicide is present in epilepsy even
without depression; mortality shoots when clinical depression is positive (nearly 25 times higher). SSRIs are the �rst line; may reduce seizure
threshold but rare. Lithium can increase seizure severity and reduces the seizure threshold.

questions.question_text: Lesions caused by an injury to which part of the brain predicts depression?
questions.explanation:
Depression (most common sequelae) and anxiety occur in roughly 1/4 of head injury survivors. Meta-analysis shows that proximity of lesion
to left frontal lobe predicts depression. Suicide risk is also higher post head injury. A schizophrenia-like psychosis with prominent paranoia is
associated with left temporal injury, while a�ective psychoses (esp. mania in 9% patients) are associated with right temporal or orbitofrontal
injury. There is also an increased prevalence of schizophrenia post head injury (-2.5% develop the disorder).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor associated with cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation:
Cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease: It is Common; poor prognosis if present at time of initial referral. Ranges from mild to severe
dementia syndrome. Risk factors are Older patients, late-onset Parkinson's disease, low socio-economic status, low education and severe
extrapyramidal signs. Lewy body dementia is closely linked pathologically; rivastigmine is useful in LBD. No drugs licensed yet for Parkinson
related dementia. Neuroleptic sensitivity is seen. Higher incidence of hallucination and delusions than Alzheimer's. Frontal executive
dysfunction - a subcortical pattern is seen.

questions.question_text: Concerning movement disorders in Parkinson's disease all are true except

options.text: They may be aggravated by psychotropic medication
Levodopa causes dose dependent psychiatric manifestations
Presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis

correct_answer.text: Presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis

questions.explanation:
Almost all patients with PD su�er from selective cognitive impairments, including di�culties with attention, concentration, problem solving,
set-shifting, and memory, which are thought to re�ect dysfunction of cortical circuits subserving frontal brain regions. These impairments
are most frequently reported by patients in terms of the disabilities they cause, such as di�culties in paying attention at work; problems
handling more than one project at a time; inability to sequence, plan, and organize tasks at work and home; and problems completing tasks
that have been started. These disabilities present serious complications for patients in the management of their everyday lives, particularly
with regard to occupational functioning(Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease - Primary Psychiatry. Retrieved from

questions.question_text: Huntington's disease is transmitted through which of the following genetic changes?

options.text: Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the long arm of chromosome 4
X-linked recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4

correct_answer.text: Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4

questions.explanation:
A single autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4 transmits Huntington's disease. There is Autosomal dominant
inheritance with 100% penetrance; thus 50% of a patient's o�spring will be a�ected. The speci�c genetic defect has been identi�ed as an
expansion of the trinucleotide sequence CAG between 37 and 120 repeats on chromosome 4.

questions.question_text: During pregnancy, where continued use of Valproate is deemed essential, what is the maximum dose recommended?
questions.explanation:
Where continued use of Valproate or carbamazepine is deemed essential, low dose monotherapy is strongly recommended, as the
teratogenic e�ect is probably dose related. NICE recommends that the dose of Valproate should be limited to 1000 mg a day. Ref: Maudsley
prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 351

questions.question_text: When used as mood stabilizers, what is the minimum period suggested to withdraw anticonvulsant drugs?
questions.explanation:
When used as mood stabilizers, it would be prudent to withdraw anticonvulsant drugs slowly. The optimum period of taper is unknown. A
period of at least 1 month is suggested. When used for epilepsy, the dose should be gradually tapered over a period of 6 months. If the
patient is taking more than one anticonvulsant, each drug should be withdrawn sequentially. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th
edition; 343

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime risk of suicide in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation:
The suicide rate for patients with Huntington's disease is 4-6 times higher than that for the general population, being as high as 12.7%, and
increasing further in those over the age of 50. Suicide is reported to be the 3rd common cause of death after pneumonia and cardiovascular
disease in patients with Huntington's disease.

questions.question_text: What is the most common behavioural change observed in patients with Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation:
The high prevalence of behavioral problems in patients with Huntington's disease was �rst recorded by Craufurd et al. in 2001. The most
common behavioral change observed in patients with Huntington's disease is lack of initiative followed by poor judgement, blunting of
a�ect, poor self-care, self-centeredness and in�exibility. Irritability, impulsivity and verbal outbursts are also reported ranging from 15 to
60% of cases. Ref: Craufurd D Thompson JC Snowden (2001); behavioral change in Huntington's disease. Neuropsychiatry and behavioral
neurology; 14: 219-226

questions.question_text: Which of the following feature is associated more with Huntington's rather than Alzheimer's dementia?

options.text: Impairment in executive function correlates with general cognitive decline

questions.explanation:
Sub cortical type of dementia is seen in Huntington's and cortical type is seen in Alzheimer's type. All the other features listed above are
more associated with Alzheimer's type. Other features of Huntington's include gradual onset, early and signi�cant impairment in executive
function, disproportionate to other cognitive domains, language function relatively preserved until late, Visuospatial function and semantic
memory relatively preserved until late. The predominant cognitive impairment in Huntington's disease is characterized by impaired
executive function.

questions.question_text: Choose an accurate statement with regard to depressive disorders in terminal illness

options.text: Presence of somatic symptoms strongly favour the diagnosis
It does not respond to antidepressants
Depression is uncommon in palliative care settings

questions.explanation:
SSRIs do not have much evidence but are widely used in depressed patients receiving palliative care. Low dose amitriptyline (avoid in
delirium risk; useful if neuropathic pain), lofepramine and rapid-acting psychostimulant such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate (in a
patient who has only weeks of life) are other useful options.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests would be required to make a diagnosis of Huntington's disease in a patient without a family history?
questions.explanation:
Sporadic appearance of new mutations is not uncommon in the Huntington disease gene. Hence a genetic test is advised even in those who
present without family history.

questions.question_text:
Mr. P has treatment resistant schizophrenia and is currently on clozapine 600 mg /day. Which anticonvulsant should be used to prevent
clozapine induced seizures?
questions.explanation: Sodium Valproate is the anticonvulsant of choice as it has a lower incidence of leucopenia than carbamazepine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about periodic limb movement disorders (PLMD) is incorrect?

options.text: Its diagnosis requires polysomnographic documentation of an increased number of PLMS in association with signi�cant disruption of
PLMS are a common phenomenon in otherwise healthy individuals.
These movements can cause clinical sleep disturbance expressed by insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness.
It is characterized by periodic episodes of repetitive and stereotyped limb movements that occur during sleep.

questions.explanation:
PLMD is characterized by periodic episodes of repetitive and stereotyped limb movements that occur during sleep. These movements can
cause clinical sleep disturbance expressed by insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness. In contrast to RLS, PLMD is not an awake
phenomenon but an asleep phenomenon, and its diagnosis requires polysomnographic documentation of an increased number of PLMS in
association with signi�cant disruption of sleep architecture and symptomatology. Polysomnographic diagnostic criteria for PLMS1 are based
on electromyography (EMG) of the right and left anterior tibialis muscles. The movements may or may not be followed by arousal or
awakening as determined by the polysomnogram. PLMS are a common phenomenon in otherwise healthy individuals. They also become
more prevalent with increasing age (occurring in up to 34% of people over 60 years of age).

questions.question_text: Many patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome will meet the criteria for another psychiatric diagnosis, which is most commonly;
questions.explanation:
Many patients with CFS will meet the criteria for another psychiatric diagnosis, most commonly major depression. Arguments exist for
calling CFS a form of atypical depression; however this is untenable in a signi�cant minority of cases. Not only do patients resist a
'psychiatric' diagnosis, but many do not have anhedonia or pervasively low mood, and attribute any mood disturbance to the restriction on
their activities caused by their illness. Nonetheless, treatment of co morbid depressive or anxiety symptoms can produce clinical
improvement. There is a high rate of depression in patient with CFS. 23% of CFS patient have current major depression and 50%- 75% have
life time history of major depression (Wessley et .al, 1998 ). Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry-753

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man with Parkinsons disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Choose the best antipsychotic:
questions.explanation:
Eight open-label studies have assessed quetiapine use in 191 patients with psychosis and Parkinson's disease, with improvement in
psychosis recorded in 152 (80%). In addition to the open-label studies, there have been two single-blind, randomized trials comparing
quetiapine and clozapine. These studies suggest that quetiapine has similar e�cacy to clozapine in controlling psychosis.

questions.question_text:
Mrs.Z has a history of bipolar depression and is on treatment with mood stabilizer throughout her pregnancy. She gave birth to a male child
with Cleft palate. The most likely o�ending drug is;
questions.explanation:
Data for Lamotrigine suggests a low risk of foetal malformation when used as monotherapy, although a substantially increased risk of cleft
palate has been reported. Clearance of Lamotrigine seems to increase radically during pregnancy. NICE suggest that Lamotrigine should not
be routinely prescribed in pregnancy.

questions.question_text: The core symptom of neurasthenia is
questions.explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is the current preferred name for a clinical syndrome whose central feature is severe fatigue, unrelated to
exertion and unrelieved by rest (neurasthenia). Fatigue is a symptom characterised by a subjective feeling of lethargy, lack of energy,
exhaustion, and a feeling of increased e�ort to do anything. Patients also complain of aching muscles, poor unrefreshing sleep, aching
joints, and headaches. They may date the symptoms very precisely to an episode of viral infection with sore throat, fever, and tender lymph
nodes. CFS is currently preferred to the names myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) and post-viral fatigue syndrome as it doesn't imply
knowledge of underlying pathology or aetiology. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry-754.
